papers.title: CLIFF: Carrying Location Information in Full Frames into Human Pose and Shape Estimation
checklist: Scope of the reported pose and translation results

checkpoints.inputs: Image-centred box coordinates (200, -100), box size 400, focal length 1000.
Same cropped appearance, same box and focal length, but centre (-200, 100).
checkpoints.expected: Geometry becomes (-0.2, 0.1, 0.4). Appearance can be held fixed, while geometry changes. An actual pose prediction requires a learned regressor.

questions.prompt: What information does resizing the crop hide?
questions.reference: Absolute location and scale of the crop relative to the full image.

questions.prompt: What is combined before regression?
questions.reference: Visual crop features and an encoding of full-image bounding-box geometry.

questions.prompt: Compute the geometry for centre (100, 50), box size 300 and focal length 1000.
questions.reference: (0.1, 0.05, 0.3) for image-centred coordinates.

papers.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
checklist: Qualify task results and parameter savings

checkpoints.inputs: Dense d_out by d_in matrix. Adapter rank r.
checkpoints.expected: Adapter elements are r(d_in+d_out), versus d_in*d_out dense matrix weights.

questions.prompt: Which parameters are frozen and which are trainable?
questions.reference: The pretrained weights W0 are frozen. The low-rank factors A and B are trained.

questions.prompt: If Ax is 4 and B is [2,-1] transposed, what update is added at scale 1?
questions.reference: The update is [8,-4] transposed.

questions.prompt: What happens when adapter scale is zero?
questions.reference: The update vanishes and the original frozen-layer output is recovered.

papers.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
checklist: Same-input branch addition and dimension handling
Reported results distinguished from toy example

checkpoints.inputs: x=[2,-1], F(x)=[-0.5,3], identity shortcut, examine the sum before activation.
Residual branch F(x)=0 and matching dimensions.

questions.prompt: What degradation problem motivates residual learning?
questions.reference: A deeper plain network can have worse training error even though it could in principle copy a shallower solution.

questions.prompt: What does F(x) represent in a residual block?
questions.reference: The residual mapping H(x)−x. The block obtains H(x) by adding the shortcut.

questions.prompt: For x=[2,-1] and F(x)=[-0.5,3], give the pre-activation sum.
What shortcut is suitable when channel dimensions differ?
questions.reference: Use a defined dimension-matching shortcut, such as a learned projection. Plain elementwise identity addition needs matching shapes.

questions.prompt: If a residual branch outputs all zeros and the shortcut is identity, what is passed into the following activation?
questions.reference: The unchanged input x.

questions.prompt: Does this hand-calculated block establish a performance gain on a benchmark?
questions.reference: It demonstrates the operation only. Performance requires the controlled experiments in the paper.

papers.title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
checklist: Novel view synthesis and scene representation
Limits of sampled or visibility-occluded evidence

checkpoints.inputs: Two ray samples with alpha values 0.5 and 0.5, grayscale colours 0.8 and 0.2, black residual background.
checkpoints.expected: Sample weights are 0.5 and 0.25. Output is 0.45 and residual transmittance is 0.25.

checkpoints.inputs: First ray sample fully opaque with colour 0.8.
checkpoints.expected: Weight of later samples becomes zero, so output is 0.8.

questions.prompt: What does NeRF predict from a queried location and direction?
questions.reference: Volume density depends on location, and emitted RGB can also depend on viewing direction.

questions.prompt: What is the role of accumulated transmittance in rendering a ray?
questions.reference: It measures the fraction that reaches a sample after nearer points, attenuating contributions behind opaque content.

questions.prompt: Two samples have alpha 0.5 and 0.5 and colours 0.8 and 0.2 with black background. What is the pixel?
What does an opaque foreground sample do to a later sample's contribution?
questions.reference: It drives the transmittance to the later sample to zero.

questions.prompt: How would using different viewing directions at the same position affect a radiance query?
questions.reference: View-dependent colour can change. In the original formulation density is a function of position.

questions.prompt: Why sample the ray at multiple points?
questions.reference: Multiple samples approximate volume integration, including where density and colour change along the ray.

papers.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
checklist: Noisy stochastic gradients and comparison baseline
Reported results separated from general claims

checkpoints.inputs: One parameter θ0=1, g1=2, β1=0.9, β2=0.999, α=0.1, moments zero, ε≈0.
checkpoints.expected: m1=0.2, v1=0.004, corrected m=2 and v=4, θ1≈0.9.

checkpoints.inputs: Same θ0, g1, α under plain SGD.

questions.prompt: What does Adam's first moment accumulate?
questions.reference: An exponential moving average of the gradients.

questions.prompt: What does its second moment accumulate?
questions.reference: An exponential moving average of squared gradients, before the square root used in the update.

questions.prompt: Why correct the bias of the moments?
questions.reference: Zero-initialized averages are biased toward zero early. Dividing by 1−β^t compensates for the missing history.

questions.prompt: With g=2, β1=0.9 and β2=0.999 at step 1, what are the uncorrected moments?
With θ=1, α=0.1, the above moments corrected, and ε negligible, compare Adam and SGD after one step.
questions.reference: Adam gives about 0.9. SGD gives 0.8.

questions.prompt: Holding the first moment fixed, what does a larger corrected second moment do to the update magnitude?
questions.reference: It enlarges the denominator and reduces the step magnitude.

papers.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
checklist: Qualify reported runtime by hardware and setup

checkpoints.expected: Softmax weights [0.25,0.75] and output 5. Tiling changes the update path while preserving the mathematical output.

checkpoints.inputs: First score tile only, then consume the larger second tile.
checkpoints.expected: Running max increases from 0 to ln(3). Scale prior denominator and numerator by 1/3 before adding the second contribution.

questions.prompt: What resource bottleneck does FlashAttention target?
questions.reference: Data movement between GPU high-bandwidth memory and on-chip SRAM.

questions.prompt: Why tile Q, K and V?
questions.reference: Tiles can be processed in on-chip memory while avoiding write-out of the full attention matrix to high-bandwidth memory.

questions.prompt: What statistics are carried when combining softmax tiles?
questions.reference: At minimum a running maximum and normalization mass, with an accumulated weighted value numerator or equivalent normalized output.

questions.prompt: For scores [0, ln(3)] and values [2,6], what is the exact result?
questions.reference: 5, from weights 1/4 and 3/4.

questions.prompt: What must happen when a new tile increases the maximum?
questions.reference: Rescale old contributions into the new maximum's exponential frame before combining them with new terms.

questions.prompt: How do the standard and tiled outputs compare in exact arithmetic?
questions.reference: They compute the same attention output. The tiled implementation changes the data movement and intermediate storage.
